body:
@jeisinger @estark37 I'd especially appreciate review of the section titled "Referrer policy attributes". There are a few concerns. Note especially.

> The empty string is also a valid keyword, and maps to the No Referrer When Downgrade state. The attribute's invalid value default and missing value default is the No Element Policy state.

My intent here is that the "No Element Policy" state is used to fall back to the Document's policy, as part of https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-referrer-policy/issues/40.

The cases I'm wondering about are:
- `<a>` (missing value default)
- `<a referrerpolicy="">` (empty string)
- `<a referrerpolicy="florble">` (invalid value default)
- `<a referrerpolicy="florble unsafe-url">` (invalid value default, as specced)
- `<a referrerpolicy="unsafe-url florble">` (invalid value default, as specced)

I note that the Referrer Policy spec says in an example:

> Suppose older user agents don’t understand the unsafe-url policy. A site can specify an origin policy followed by an unsafe-url policy: older user agents will ignore the unknown unsafe-url value and use origin, while newer user agents will use unsafe-url because it is the last to be processed. 

But in the case of HTML attributes I don't see this reflected normatively anywhere. The whole way in which HTML attributes get mapped to states does not allow multiple tokens in the attribute where we pick the first valid one.

Another interesting thing to note is that the spec does not use "Determine token's policy" for content attributes, so the older values of "never", "default", and "always" count as invalid. This seems to be intended, looking at Chrome's code.

@mikewest move to `<meta name>`, and also spelled out more explicitly how multiple such elements interact---I went with the `theme-color` model. A few notes/questions:
- I went with "in a document" instead of Chrome's "in a shadow-including document" since that seems to make much more sense. I can file a Chrome bug for this if you agree.
- "Determine token’s Policy" returning the empty string on failure, instead of null, is pretty weird.
- The special-casing of `<meta name="referrer" value="">` is a bit weird. Could "Determine token’s Policy" return null for the empty string, instead of returning No Referrer?

> I note that the Referrer Policy spec says in an example:
> 
> > Suppose older user agents don’t understand the unsafe-url policy. A site can specify an origin policy followed by an unsafe-url policy: older user agents will ignore the unknown unsafe-url value and use origin, while newer user agents will use unsafe-url because it is the last to be processed.
> 
> But in the case of HTML attributes I don't see this reflected normatively anywhere. The whole way in which HTML attributes get mapped to states does not allow multiple tokens in the attribute where we pick the first valid one.

Hrm. I think it would be fine to say that the example you quoted applies to Document policies delivered via HTTP header or meta, but not to referrerpolicy attributes. Authors could always do feature detection to dynamically set referrerpolicy attributes, right? So for the attributes they shouldn't really need to rely on being able to supply multiple tokens and the first valid one getting picked. If you agree, I can update the Referrer Policy spec to say that that example only applies to Document policies and that authors should use feature detection to deploy new policy values in referrerpolicy attributes.

> "Determine token’s Policy" returning the empty string on failure, instead of null, is pretty weird.

Can you elaborate on this a bit? I don't think I understand the concern. It was changed to empty string to address https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-referrer-policy/issues/21... but I feel like I'm missing some nuance here.

> The special-casing of <meta name="referrer" value=""> is a bit weird. Could "Determine token’s Policy" return null for the empty string, instead of returning No Referrer?

Hm, I'm not sure why it is that why and I think it predates my time working on referrer policy. Maybe @jeisinger or @mikewest knows?

> Another interesting thing to note is that the spec does not use "Determine token's policy" for content attributes, so the older values of "never", "default", and "always" count as invalid. This seems to be intended, looking at Chrome's code.

I would believe that this was intentional, though I think this part of the spec also predates me. The `referrerpolicy` attribute was only implemented pretty recently, so there might have been no need to support the older keywords.

> Hrm. I think it would be fine to say that the example you quoted applies to Document policies delivered via HTTP header or meta, but not to referrerpolicy attributes.

Yeah, I think that's fine. I just wanted to check to make sure that was the intended behavior.

> Can you elaborate on this a bit? I don't think I understand the concern. It was changed to empty string to address w3c/webappsec-referrer-policy#21... but I feel like I'm missing some nuance here.

I am not sure what @annevk's intention was in filing w3c/webappsec-referrer-policy#21, but maybe it was to try and align with Fetch, who does not separate the notion of states (like `No Referrer When Downgrade`) and strings (like "`no-referrer-when-downgrade`")?

I expected the natural model to be that "Determine token's policy" always returns a policy, not sometimes a policy and sometimes a string. It seems to me like the spec could be clarified by replacing the empty string idea with something like a `Default` policy. (Or null, but maybe `Default` would be clearer.) In general the `Default` policy means "fall back to some higher level referrer policy", or if there is no such higher-level policy, it means `No Referrer When Downgrade`.

If you agree, I would like to do a small pull request to Referrer Policy that makes this change, and then this PR can build on top of that.

Alternately, we could align with Fetch and get rid of the separation between states (`No Referrer When Downgrade`) and strings ("`no-referrer-when-downgrade`"). Let me know which of those you prefer.

Or we can continue with having policies be sometimes states and sometimes the empty string, but that seems a bit messy :).

> Hm, I'm not sure why it is that why and I think it predates my time working on referrer policy. Maybe @jeisinger or @mikewest knows?

So, here is the current behavior, as best as I understand it:
- `<meta name="referrer" content="">` is completely ignored. The meta tag has no impact on referrer policy.
- `Referrer-Policy:` HTTP header (i.e. a header with no value) will set a `No Referrer` policy.

If this behavior is intentional, then I guess the current setup is fine. I want to check that it is, though.

## 

In any case, thanks for the review! Maybe @annevk could give it a look too, for editorial issues and such.

Note to self: I think I made a mistake, and `<a referrerpolicy="">` should use the `Default` policy (aka the empty string), not `No Referrer When Downgrade`.

> Alternately, we could align with Fetch and get rid of the separation between states (No Referrer When Downgrade) and strings ("no-referrer-when-downgrade"). Let me know which of those you prefer.

I would personally prefer Referrer Policy to do this. For a long time I tried to have a difference between strings and states and it always leads to confusion and subtle issues. It's much easier to keep things straight if there is no distinction.
Very nice PR overall. Great to see this integration becoming more tightly defined.
Code review addressed. Waiting to hear how we want to define states: all strings, all states, or mostly states + the empty string. Tagging "do not merge yet" until we get that sorted out.

> `<meta name="referrer" content="">` is completely ignored. The meta tag has no impact on referrer policy.
> Referrer-Policy: HTTP header (i.e. a header with no value) will set a No Referrer policy.
> If this behavior is intentional, then I guess the current setup is fine. I want to check that it is, though.

That seems weird to me, though I can't say whether it's intentional or not.

> Alternately, we could align with Fetch and get rid of the separation between states (No Referrer When Downgrade) and strings ("no-referrer-when-downgrade"). Let me know which of those you prefer.

That seems reasonable to me and I'll trust @annevk's judgement that it's the least likely to cause subtle problems.

@annevk this is now ready to merge, updated to use referrer policy's latest stuff. (And I'd like to merge it ASAP since referrer policy removed their content and IDL attributes in favor of this PR... there was a bit of a two-sided patch situation there.)
This looks fine, assuming https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-referrer-policy/issues/40 is indeed going to be addressed later as that is clearly missing.
